source.title: Beyond accuracy: generalization properties of bio-plausible temporal credit assignment rules
source.authors: Y. Liu; Arna Ghosh; B. Richards; Eric T. Shea-Brown; Guillaume Lajoie

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper and appendices; no garbling or truncation is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures train–test generalization gaps and tests their association with loss curvature using recurrent networks trained with approximate versus exact gradients. These are different models, learning rules, tasks, and curvature measures from the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The study tests generalization gaps and their relation to curvature in RNNs trained with different temporal credit assignment rules. It does not test random-label memorization, width beyond interpolation, convolution versus fully connected image classifiers, optimizer comparisons, batch-size effects, dropout, or removal of memorized examples. Figure-only comparisons are recorded without reconstructing numerical values.
record.test_reason: The study uses the flatness–generalization literature to analyze temporal credit assignment rules in RNNs. Its own results concern generalization gaps and Hessian curvature, not V7's magnitude-scaled perturbation measure or its ranking against norm and margin measures. None of V1–V8 is directly tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially correct. The authors report worse and more variable generalization for the tested bio-plausible rules, higher curvature, and a significant but imperfect curvature–gap association. Their theoretical explanation is conditional: small along-gradient steps permit higher-curvature convergence, while orthogonal approximation error constrains stable learning rates. Sequential MNIST training performance is not matched: the three-factor rule reaches about 70% training accuracy.
record.recipe_differences: Recurrent networks trained with temporal gradient approximations versus exact BPTT; tasks include sequential MNIST and two neuroscience-inspired tasks, not the image-classification and random-label settings in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Learning rule and task affect the reported generalization gaps and curvature; early stopping and learning-rate scheduling alter the comparison. Curvature convergence was also observed with Adam, though SGD was used for the main matching-step experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: The tested bio-plausible temporal credit assignment rules produce worse and more variable generalization gaps than BPTT. Early-stopped BPTT has a gap of 0.2 ± 0.1 versus 0.5 ± 0.3 for the three-factor rule on sequential MNIST.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Temporal gradient approximations can worsen generalization relative to BPTT in the tested recurrent-network tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: Leading Hessian eigenvalue correlates significantly but imperfectly with generalization gap, and approximate rules tend toward higher curvature. The early-stopping comparison reports 2550 ± 490 for the three-factor rule versus 316 ± 84 for BPTT.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Leading Hessian curvature is associated with generalization gaps in these recurrent-network tasks, with substantial unexplained variability.

fits_no_version.finding: Reducing BPTT's along-gradient step length worsens generalization; initially larger learning rates followed by decay slightly improve the three-factor rule's gap without eliminating its disadvantage.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Along-gradient step length and learning-rate scheduling affect generalization in these temporal credit assignment experiments.

record.problems: The tested systems are RNNs on three sequence and neuroscience-inspired tasks, not the architectures and data conditions specified in the claim versions. The authors note that the generalization-gap/curvature relationship is messy and offers limited predictive power; Hessian flatness is a local, scale-dependent measure. Most plotted values are not numerically stated in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: No rows left out. Figure-only values were retained as figure-only; numeric reconstruction from plots was not attempted.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, natural-label held-out accuracy, and their coexistence under the same architecture and recipe.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning. Appendix Figure 11 reports curvature trends with Adam, not comparative held-out performance.
Large-batch held-out penalties under fixed epoch budgets and their recovery through recipe changes. Batch-size tuning is not a reported test of these effects.
Dropout interventions, small-data failures, excessive-dropout underfitting, and removal of dropout with weight decay.

Magnitude-scaled weight-perturbation tolerance and its ranking of generalization gaps against norm and margin measures among similarly fitted networks. Hessian eigenvalues, spectral decay, and readout-weight relative flatness are different measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: All rows retain versions ["none"]. Their cannot_determine states concern applicability to V1–V8, not whether the paper reports the unrelated effects. Appendix Figures 7 and 8 corroborate curvature trends with spectral decay and readout-weight relative flatness; neither supplies V7's specified perturbation measure or ranking comparison, so neither requires a version-linked missing entry.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label test generalization.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD held-out performance.
Large versus small batches under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.

Magnitude-scaled weight perturbation sharpness and its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures; the study instead measures leading Hessian eigenvalues, power-law decay, and relative flatness in RNN tasks.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.
